summary: I searched for prior art on learning-curve extrapolation, sample-size planning in chemometrics and spectroscopy, deterministic-equivalent and GP learning-curve theory, GCV/KARE-type risk estimators, data-requirement and scaling-law forecasting, high-dimensional noise estimation, and patents. I found no publication or patent that fits deterministic-equivalent ridge risk to a small labelled pilot's grouped CV regularisation path to forecast absolute calibration RMSE at larger n. The closest patent, US11593655B2, covers power-law data-requirement prediction, i.e. the baseline family. The novelty claims as written are overstated, however, and the closest prior art is misdescribed. Wei, Hu & Steinhardt (2022), cited only as a 'current-n' estimator, already use the ridge path mapped to kappa to estimate the alignment and eigendecay exponents, predict scaling exponents, fit the r = 1 two-parameter deterministic equivalent, and find the r < 1 regularity on real data. The central 'identifiability limit' contradicts established estimators of noise variance and SNR in high-dimensional linear models (Dicker 2014; EigenPrism 2017; Kong & Valiant 2018). The manuscript's own data point to a precision limit at n0 = 25 rather than non-identifiability. The chemometric theory of prediction error vs n and eigen-structure (Næs & Martens 1988; Helland & Almøy 1994; Nadler & Coifman 2005) and RMT use in chemometrics (Kritchman & Nadler 2008) are not cited. Nor are the ACA sample-size-planning paper of Beleites et al. (2013), the ML data-requirement literature that already reported optimistic power-law extrapolation and cross-task corrections (Mahmood et al. 2022; Jain et al. 2023), or the GP learning-curve and empirical-Bayes route (Sollich; Le Gratiet & Garnier 2015), which the paper's own ablation does not beat after Holm correction. What remains novel and valuable is a carefully leakage-controlled, pre-registered 38-task benchmark. It shows that the pilot's CV error, alone or with a transferred slope, forecasts as well as any extrapolation. The paper should be repositioned around that.
strengths: No publication or patent was found that performs exactly the proposed pilot-based fit of deterministic-equivalent ridge risk to a grouped LOGO regularisation path for calibration learning curves, so a narrower novelty claim is defensible.

The benchmark is large (38 tasks, 6 sources, 2,640 pilots), leakage-controlled (group-disjoint splits, replicate averaging, LOGO) and pre-registered, with post-hoc additions time-stamped and negative results reported (EXPERIMENT_LOG.md; Sections 3.6 and 4.4).
Trivial but strong competitors (FLAT, SLOPE-T) are included, and the paper openly reports that they match or beat the proposed method (Table 2).

issues.title: The closest prior art (Wei, Hu & Steinhardt 2022, ref. [25]) is misdescribed and already anticipates the path-to-kappa idea, the two-parameter isotropic fit and the 'r < 1' finding
issues.description: The Introduction and the novelty map say that GCV/KARE-type estimators, including ref. [25], estimate risk only 'at the current sample size, not at a larger one', and that 'the theory has not been turned into a forecasting tool'. That is not what ref. [25] does. Wei et al. (ICML 2022, arXiv:2203.06176) (a) estimate the eigendecay exponent and the alignment exponent of the target from empirically observable training-set quantities. Their Prop. 5 does this from the ridge regularisation path at fixed N, mapped onto the effective regularisation kappa(lambda, N), which is the same path-to-kappa mapping that defines RPM. (b) They combine the two exponents to predict the learning-curve (scaling-law) exponent of optimally tuned ridge and check it against the observed rates on real data (their Table 3). (c) Their 'spectrum-only' estimator (App. E.2/F) is the Dobriban–Wager deterministic equivalent under an isotropic prior N(0, alpha^2 I). That is exactly RPM's r = 1 model, and alpha^2 and sigma^2 are fitted by least squares over (N, lambda) pairs. (d) They report delta-hat < 0 'for all datasets'. With lambda_i ~ i^-(1+gamma) and (beta'v_i)^2 ~ i^-delta, the manuscript's exponent is r = 1 + delta/(1+gamma), so delta < 0 is exactly r < 1. The headline finding that 'the analyte signal extended into weak spectral modes in every task' is therefore the same empirical regularity Wei et al. reported for real representations. Ref. [25] is also wrongly labelled a 'kernel-alignment risk estimator'; it is a GCV paper. What remains new is narrower: an absolute RMSE forecast at larger n with finite-n and intercept prefactors, from a small labelled pilot's grouped LOGO path, with the eigen-spectrum from unlabelled spectra, benchmarked on spectroscopic calibrations. The manuscript does not claim this narrower contribution and does not compare against the prior-art estimator.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md l.26 ('Related estimators such as generalised cross-validation (GCV) [23] and the kernel-alignment risk estimator [24,25] estimate the risk at the current sample size, not at a larger one. To our knowledge, the theory has not been turned into a forecasting tool'); Supplementary Note 3 (supplementary_full.md l.938, l.956: 'KARE / GCV (Jacot 2020; Wei 2022) | Risk at the current n'); Abstract l.13 and Section 4.2 l.166 (r < 1 presented as a finding). Wei et al. arXiv:2203.06176 Sec. 6.2: Prop. 4 (gamma from the slope of log N^-1 Tr((XX^T)^-1) vs log N), Prop. 5 (y^T(XX^T+N lambda I)^-1 y ~ kappa(lambda,N)^-(1-delta)/(1+gamma)), Table 3 (alpha-hat = gamma-hat + delta-hat vs actual alpha), text: 'we observe for all datasets that delta-hat < 0'; App. E.2: 'we fit alpha^2 and sigma^2 to minimize the mean squared error of the estimates over the set of (N, lambda) pairs'.
issues.corrective_action: 1. Rewrite the related-work paragraph (l.26), the contributions list (l.28) and Supplementary Note 3 so that Wei et al. is described correctly: path-based estimation of eigendecay and alignment exponents, prediction of scaling exponents, and r < 1 on real data. 2. Remove 'not turned into a forecasting tool' and the KARE label for [25]. 3. State the actual increment explicitly (pilot-scale, absolute-level forecast, grouped LOGO, unlabelled covariance, finite-n prefactor, chemometric benchmark). 4. Present the r < 1 result as a confirmation in spectroscopic data of a regularity previously seen in ML representations. 5. Add the Wei et al. exponent estimator as a baseline.
issues.proposed_experiment: Prior-art baseline 'WHS-slope': on the same 2,640 pilots, estimate gamma from the unlabelled-pool eigen-spectrum and delta from the pilot's ridge path via Wei et al. Prop. 5. Forecast RMSE(n) = RMSE_CV(n0) * (n/n0)^(-(gamma+delta)/2), with the noisy-regime correction if needed. Report it in Table 2 with the same Holm-corrected paired tests against RPM, RPM-w, SLOPE-T and FLAT.

issues.title: The 'identifiability limit' (the noise floor cannot be identified from a pilot) is stated as a fact but contradicts established results on noise-variance and SNR estimation in high-dimensional linear models
issues.description: Section 2.4 states that 'No pilot, however analysed, can separate target power hidden in weak modes from irreducible noise without such an assumption'. The Abstract says the noise fraction is something 'a pilot set cannot identify', and the Conclusions recommend replicate reference analyses as the route to the noise floor. No proof or citation is given, and the claim conflicts with a mature literature. (i) Dicker (Biometrika 2014, 101:269–284) gives consistent, asymptotically normal method-of-moments estimators of the residual variance and the explained-variance fraction when p/n is a non-vanishing constant, with Gaussian design and no sparsity; Dicker & Erdogdu (AISTATS 2016) give ML versions. (ii) Janson, Barber & Candès (EigenPrism, JRSSB 2017, 79:1037–1065) give confidence intervals for ||beta||^2 and for the noise level for p > n, with no sparsity and no known noise level. (iii) Kong & Valiant (NeurIPS 2018) show that the unexplained variance of the best linear predictor is estimable with O(sqrt(d)) samples (sublinear in d), with bounds that depend on the covariance's condition number when the covariance is unknown; here the covariance is available from the unlabelled spectra, as the manuscript stresses. (iv) Cortes et al. (NIPS 1993/1994) estimate the asymptotic error from small-n training and test learning curves. Even trivially, when n0 > p + 1 the OLS residual variance RSS/(n0 − p − 1) estimates the best-linear-predictor residual variance. This holds for the Mango (p = 94) and Neospectra (p = 150) tasks at n0 = 200. The manuscript's own evidence shows a precision limit, not non-identifiability: the sigma^2 collapse of RPM-T occurred in 21% of pilots at n0 = 25, 3% at n0 = 50 and none at n0 >= 100. The failure belongs to one least-squares path fit with a transferred r. The 'cannot predict' half of the title and the planning advice rest on this over-statement.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md l.82 (Section 2.4 quote), l.13 (Abstract: 'irreducible-noise fraction, which a pilot set cannot identify'), l.206 (collapse rates 21%/3%/0% by n0), l.274 (Limitation 2), l.281 (Conclusions: 'Better forecasts will require independent information on the noise floor, for example replicate reference analyses'); Table 1 l.151 and l.150 (p = 94 and 150, max n 1600 and 800, so n0 = 200 pilots exist). None of Dicker, Janson et al., Kong & Valiant or Cortes et al. is cited (grep of manuscript_full.md and supplementary_full.md returns 0 hits).
issues.corrective_action: 1. Replace 'identifiability limit' with a quantified weak-identification statement, e.g. the Fisher information or the CRLB for sigma^2 under the RPM model as a function of n0/p and the eigen-spectrum. 2. Cite and discuss the high-dimensional variance-estimation literature. 3. Remove 'however analysed' and the claim that only replicate reference analyses can inform the noise floor. 4. Test whether a statistical noise-floor estimator rescues the transferred-exponent forecaster before concluding that pilots cannot reveal it.
issues.proposed_experiment: On the existing pilots, compute a Dicker-type moment estimator (or EigenPrism) of sigma^2/var(y), using the pool covariance from unlabelled spectra for whitening. Report its error against the large-sample noise fraction by n0. Then refit RPM-T and RPM-wT with sigma^2 constrained to that estimate, or given an informative prior centred on it. Report Table-2 metrics, and the collapse rate of Section 4.4 for n0 = 25–200.

issues.title: The chemometric theory of calibration prediction error as a function of n and eigen-structure is ignored, and the claim that the theory 'has not been exploited in chemometrics' is too broad
issues.description: The manuscript presents random-matrix and eigen-structure risk theory as new to chemometrics. Chemometrics has a long tradition of exactly this kind of analysis. Næs & Martens (J. Chemom. 1988, 2:155–167) derived prediction-error formulae for PCR vs OLS in NIR analysis: bias from omitted low-variance components plus a variance term growing with components/n. This is the hard-threshold analogue of N(kappa) and df2(kappa)/n in Eq. (3). Helland & Almøy (JASA 1994, 89:583–591) and Almøy (CSDA 1996) computed asymptotic prediction errors of PCR, PLS and ridge with random X as functions of n, the eigenvalues and the 'relevant components'. Nadler & Coifman (J. Chemom. 2005, 19:107–118) gave an 'asymptotically exact' analysis of CLS/PLS prediction error with finite n in p dimensions, with extra terms ~ sigma^2 p^2/n^2 that dominate in the large-p, small-n regime typical of spectroscopy; that is itself a theoretical calibration learning curve. Random-matrix theory proper is used in chemometrics, e.g. Kritchman & Nadler (Chemom. Intell. Lab. Syst. 2008, 94:19–32; Marchenko–Pastur/Tracy–Widom rank estimation). Saccenti & Timmerman (J. Proteome Res. 2016) addressed sample-size determination for PCA/PLS-DA. Jolliffe (Appl. Stat. 1982, 31:300–303) and the relevant-component literature had established that low-variance directions can carry the response. That anticipates qualitatively the 'signal in weak modes' message. None of these is cited.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md l.26 ('it has not been exploited in chemometrics'), l.58 (mechanism of the learning curve presented as new), l.166 (weak-mode finding); reference list l.306–384 contains none of the above (grep for Næs/Naes, Helland, Nadler, Kritchman, Saccenti returns 0 hits).
issues.corrective_action: Add a paragraph linking Eq. (3) to the classical PCR/PLS prediction-error formulae: soft vs hard thresholding of eigen-modes, relevant components. Narrow the novelty claim to 'deterministic-equivalent ridge risk has not been used to forecast calibration learning curves from pilot data'. Cite Kritchman & Nadler and Nadler & Coifman as prior RMT and high-dimensional analyses in chemometrics. Present the weak-mode finding as a quantitative confirmation of a known phenomenon.

issues.title: Prior sample-size-planning work in spectroscopy is missing, including an Analytica Chimica Acta paper on the same planning problem
issues.description: Beleites et al., 'Sample size planning for classification models' (Anal. Chim. Acta 760 (2013) 25–33), used learning curves to plan the sample size of spectroscopic (Raman) models. It showed that the random uncertainty of small test sets can mask the learning curve altogether. That anticipates, for classification, the manuscript's own explanation of why sample-size decisions are ill-conditioned: 'a factor-two error in n corresponds to a smaller change in RMSE than the sampling error of a small pilot's own cross-validated RMSE'. Ramirez-Lopez et al. (Geoderma 226–227 (2014) 140–150) proposed an unsupervised, spectra-only criterion for an adequate calibration-set size in soil vis-NIR. That is directly relevant because RPM's selling point is the use of cheap unlabelled spectra. Kuang & Mouazen appears in the literature matrix but not in the reference list. The heuristic guidance the Introduction mentions (minimum sample numbers relative to model complexity) is not referenced, e.g. ASTM E1655. The historical statement that learning-curve extrapolation was 'introduced to analytical chemistry ... by Ali et al. [8]' omits Beleites et al. 2013, published in this journal.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md l.22 (heuristic guidance named without a citation), l.24 ('introduced to analytical chemistry for Raman classification by Ali et al. [8]'), l.214 (ill-conditioning argument); supplementary_full.md l.933 (Kuang & Mouazen listed but not in references); grep for Beleites, Ramirez, ASTM returns 0 hits.
issues.corrective_action: 1. Cite and discuss Beleites et al. 2013, credit it for the precision argument of Section 4.5 and correct the history in l.24. 2. Cite Ramirez-Lopez et al. 2014 and state how RPM's use of unlabelled spectra differs from spectra-only set-size criteria. 3. Cite the standard sample-number guidance (ASTM E1655 / ISO 12099) for the heuristics mentioned in l.22. 4. Optionally, score the Ramirez-Lopez criterion on the existing decision metric.

issues.title: The optimism of power-law extrapolation and the cross-task correction remedy are known from the data-requirement literature; the baselines cover only the oldest prior art, so 'should be abandoned' goes too far
issues.description: Two headline messages are presented as new: power-law extrapolation from small pilots is systematically optimistic, and a correction learned on other data sets (SLOPE-T, leave-one-source-out conformal bands) fixes it. Mahmood et al. (CVPR 2022, 'How Much More Data Do I Need?') showed that power-law, root and logarithmic regressions systematically under-estimate data requirements, i.e. they are optimistic. Their remedy was a correction factor tau learned on previous tasks; SLOPE-T and the cross-data-set band calibration are domain instances of that remedy. Jain et al. (CVPR 2023) showed that log-error vs log-size is non-linear in the small-data regime. They proposed a meta-learned piecewise power law with a confidence bound that limits the prediction horizon. Cortes et al. (NIPS 1993) and Hoiem et al. (ICML 2021) give constrained/extended power-law extrapolators. The manuscript cites LC-PFN [12] but does not test it. The comparison is restricted to unconstrained IPL3/IPL2/EXP3/LOG2 fits to a within-pilot sub-sampling curve (for n0 = 25 the subsets have about 6–21 samples). That is the weakest form of the prior-art approach, and the strong recommendation to abandon power-law extrapolation is not justified against the modern variants. A patent search found US11593655B2 ('Predicting deep learning scaling'), which covers power-law data-requirement prediction (the baseline family), not RPM.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md l.15 (Abstract: 'Power-law extrapolation from small pilot sets should be abandoned'), l.106–109 (baselines), l.123 (SLOPE-T), l.125 and l.210 (cross-data-set calibration), l.269 (recommendation i); code/src/models/forecasters.py pilot_subsample_curve (fractions 0.25–0.85 of the pilot) and CURVES; grep for Mahmood, Jain, Cortes, Hoiem returns 0 hits.
issues.corrective_action: 1. Cite and position against Mahmood et al. 2022, Jain et al. 2023, Cortes et al. 1993 and Hoiem et al. 2021. 2. Credit SLOPE-T and the calibrated bands as instances of cross-task correction rather than new rules. 3. Limit the 'abandon' recommendation to unconstrained curve fits to within-pilot sub-sampling curves unless stronger variants are also shown to fail.
issues.proposed_experiment: On the same pilots, add (a) IPL3 with its exponent and asymptote fraction given a prior learned leave-one-source-out (meta-learned power law), (b) Mahmood-style IPL3 with a LOSO-learned correction factor, and (c) LC-PFN [12] applied to the within-pilot curve. Report Table-2 metrics and the decision metric.

issues.title: The established empirical-Bayes route (GP learning-curve theory with hyperparameters estimated from the pilot) is uncited, and the paper's own ablation does not show that path matching beats it
issues.description: Eq. (2) is the self-consistent learning-curve approximation of Gaussian-process regression (Sollich, NIPS 1998/1999; Sollich & Halees, Neural Comput. 2002, 14:1393–1428). With a linear kernel and isotropic prior, GP regression is ridge with r = 1. Fitting the prior amplitude and noise by marginal likelihood and inserting them in the learning-curve formula is therefore the textbook theory-based forecast. Le Gratiet & Garnier (Machine Learning 2015, 98:407–433; arXiv:1210.2879) used GP learning-curve asymptotics to determine the observation budget needed for a target precision. So 'theory-based learning-curve forecasting from initial data' has precedent. The element that is new here is the estimator, regularisation-path matching, which replaces type-II ML. The paper's own pre-registered ablation does not establish that this estimator is better: type-II ML gave 0.305 vs 0.242, Δ = +0.063 with bootstrap CI +0.007 to +0.129, but Holm p = 1.000. That comparison used only n0 in {50, 100} and 10 pilots per task, and the type-II ML variant does not appear in the main comparison.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md l.225 (Table 3: 'type-II maximum likelihood instead of path matching | 38 | 0.305 | +0.063 | +0.007 to +0.129 | 1.000'), l.235 ('Type-II maximum likelihood instead of path matching ... made small differences'); code/src/models/forecasters.py fit_ml2 (r = 1 marginal likelihood); grep for Sollich, Gratiet returns 0 hits.
issues.corrective_action: 1. Cite the GP learning-curve literature and Le Gratiet & Garnier. 2. Describe the type-II-ML forecaster as the prior-art baseline it is. 3. Phrase the novelty claim around the path-matching estimator, supported by a properly powered head-to-head comparison.
issues.proposed_experiment: Run the type-II-ML forecaster (with the same unlabelled eigen-spectrum and Bayesian bootstrap) on the full main design: all n0 in {25, 50, 100, 200}, 20 pilots per task. Report it in Table 2 with Holm-corrected paired tests against RPM and RPM-w.

issues.title: The new method adds no demonstrated value over trivial rules, so the novelty should be framed as a benchmark and a negative result
issues.description: Contribution (ii) presents RPM as a new forecaster, and recommendation (vi) calls RPM-w 'far more reliable than curve-shape extrapolation'. On the paper's own results, the pre-registered RPM is not better than reporting the pilot's CV error. FLAT scored 0.266 vs 0.284 for RPM; RPM was better on only 15 of 38 tasks (39.5%), Holm p = 0.149. RPM is significantly worse than SLOPE-T (0.251, Holm p = 0.031). In the post-hoc gain analysis, which isolates what a forecast adds beyond the pilot's own error, RPM (0.231) is indistinguishable from predicting zero gain (FLAT 0.245, Holm p = 1.000) and from IPL3 (0.232, Holm p = 1.000), with a bias of +0.209. For sample-size decisions RPM was correct in 4.7% and 2.0% of pilots, against 25.1% and 9.2% for IPL3 and 29.5% and 21.1% for SLOPE-T. FLAT, which needs no theory at all, also beats IPL3. RPM's advantage over the power-law baselines therefore comes from not forecasting optimistic improvement, not from extracting information via the theory. The publishable novelty is the leakage-controlled 38-task benchmark and the negative result, not a forecasting tool.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md l.28 (contribution ii), l.176, l.188–189 (Table 2 FLAT and IPL3 rows), l.198, l.214 (gain and decision results), l.269 (recommendation vi); results/numbers.json: pct_tasks_rpm_better_than_flat = 39.47, posthoc_gain (RPM mean_task_gain_abs_err 0.231, bias +0.209), posthoc_gain_stats (RPM vs IPL3 p_holm = 1.0).
issues.corrective_action: Reframe the Abstract, contributions and title emphasis around the benchmark finding: the pilot CV error plus a transferred slope is as good as any theory-based extrapolation. Present RPM as a theoretically motivated but non-superior forecaster. Delete or qualify recommendation (vi): RPM-w is not significantly better than FLAT, and FLAT is also 'far more reliable than curve-shape extrapolation'.

issues.title: Contribution (i) mostly confirms known theory, and the claimed noise-floor-governs-slope regularity is confounded by how far each curve extends
issues.description: The kappa-collapse (Fig. 2b) follows directly from Eq. (2). The equivalence of (n, mu) pairs with equal effective regularisation, with data-driven estimation of the equivalence paths, was established by Patil & Du (NeurIPS 2023). Wei et al. (2022, Fig. 4) showed GCV/deterministic-equivalent agreement across N and lambda on real data. The noise dependence of learning-curve exponents (a crossover from noiseless to noisy rates) is the subject of Cui et al. (NeurIPS 2021) and is shown on real data there. The alignment exponent is the classical source-condition exponent (Caponnetto & De Vito, Found. Comput. Math. 2007), which is not mentioned. These should be cited and the results presented as domain confirmation. Moreover, the 'dominant' role of the noise fraction is not cleanly established. In results/numbers.json (slope_spearman), the slope correlates more strongly with pool size (Spearman rho = +0.62) than with the noise fraction (+0.59). Pool size determines how far the ground-truth curve extends, and curves flatten at large n. I recomputed from alignment_exponents.csv and slope_per_doubling.csv: noise fraction and pool size are themselves correlated (rho = +0.55, p = 0.0004). The partial Spearman correlation of slope with noise fraction given pool size is only 0.38. Among the 24 tasks with pools > 1000, rho = 0.38 (p = 0.064). Across tasks the fitted r and the noise fraction are also strongly anti-correlated (rho = −0.68, p = 2e−6), which suggests the large-sample (r, sigma^2) estimates trade off. No uncertainty is reported for r.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md l.28 (contribution i), l.160 (kappa-collapse), l.166 and l.170 (alignment and slope claims, R^2 = 0.73 model omits curve range); results/numbers.json slope_spearman; recomputation from results/alignment_exponents.csv and results/slope_per_doubling.csv (scratch script under /tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R1/).
issues.corrective_action: Cite Patil & Du 2023, Cui et al. 2021 and Caponnetto & De Vito 2007, and reframe (i) as domain validation. Recompute slopes over a common n-range for all tasks (e.g. 50–800 or 50–400), or add log(max n) or log(n_pool) to the slope regression. Report bootstrap or profile-likelihood intervals for r and for the noise fraction. This is a reanalysis of the existing ground-truth curves, not a new experiment.

issues.title: Recent random-matrix work on cross-validation across sample sizes, correlated samples and finite-n validity is uncited, so the justification of key implementation choices is missing
issues.description: Several recent works bear directly on RPM's design and are not cited. Liu & Dobriban (ICLR 2020) used deterministic-equivalent theory to correct K-fold CV for the mismatch between training size n(K−1)/K and n, i.e. to transport the risk and penalty between sample sizes; this is a direct precursor of the transport step in RPM. Atanasov, Zavatone-Veth & Pehlevan (arXiv:2408.04607, 2024) analyse ridge risk and (G)CV with correlated samples. That is directly relevant because the pilots contain grouped soil layers and RPM uses an ad-hoc n_eff = n0 − mean group size. Non-asymptotic deterministic equivalents (Misiakiewicz & Saeed, arXiv:2403.08938; Cheng & Montanari 2024; Defilippis, Loureiro & Misiakiewicz, arXiv:2405.15699) are needed to justify applying an asymptotic formula at n0 = 25. Karkada et al. (arXiv:2510.14878, ICLR 2026) predict kernel learning curves from raw data statistics. The code docstring cites Simon et al. (2023, TMLR, eigenlearning), but that reference is absent from the manuscript.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md l.44 (refs [15,16,18] only), l.65–69 (path to kappa mapping), Methods give no justification of n_eff; code/src/models/forecasters.py RPMForecaster.fit_forecast (n_eff = n0 − gsz); code/src/models/theory.py docstring (cites Simon et al. 2023, TMLR).
issues.corrective_action: Cite and briefly discuss these works. Justify the n_eff correction with the correlated-sample theory, or replace it with that theory's correction. Cite non-asymptotic results, or show by simulation that Eq. (3) remains accurate at n0 = 25 with p = 100–216.

issues.title: Conformal calibration and closed-form grouped deletion are used without the standard references
issues.description: The calibrated bands are described as 'split-conformal calibration across data sets', but no conformal-prediction reference is given (e.g. Vovk, Gammerman & Shafer 2005; Lei et al., JASA 2018). The exchangeability-across-tasks assumption that the leave-one-source-out calibration needs is not stated. The NIR group-conformal paper listed in Supplementary Note 3 (Talanta 2026, doi:10.1016/j.talanta.2026.130941) is not cited. The closed-form leave-one-group-out residuals (I − H_gg)^{-1} e_g are classical (Allen 1974 PRESS; Cook & Weisberg 1982) and should be credited.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md l.65, l.125, l.210; supplementary_full.md l.940; reference list l.306–384 (no conformal reference).
issues.corrective_action: Add the references, state the across-task exchangeability assumption behind the LOSO conformal bands, and cite the classical grouped-deletion identity.

issues.title: The literature matrix (Supplementary Note 3) does not match the reference list and contains internal project material
issues.description: Supplementary Note 3 cites works that are absent from the reference list: Kuang & Mouazen 2014, Bouckaert et al. 2011, Faber & Kowalski 1997, Simon et al. 2021 and the Talanta 2026 paper. It also contains a 'Topic-selection record' listing screened research directions ('crowded in ACA 2026', 'generic-DL risk'), which is project-management material, not supplementary science. The main text twice describes SLOPE-T as 'suggested by the hostile-reviewer check', which is internal jargon that readers will not understand.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md l.123 and l.198 ('hostile-reviewer check'); manuscript/build/supplementary_full.md l.918–962 (Supplementary Note 3, including the topic-selection record at l.962).
issues.corrective_action: Remove the topic-selection record. Reconcile the literature matrix with the reference list and correct the Wei et al. entry (see R1-C01-01). Describe SLOPE-T as 'a simple transferred-slope competitor added after pre-registration'.

recommendation_rationale: Within my remit the problems are positioning and the correctness of the claims, not fatal flaws in the experiments. The closest prior art (ref. [25]) is misdescribed. The 'identifiability limit' is stated as a theorem but contradicted by existing high-dimensional variance estimators. Large relevant literatures are uncited: chemometric prediction-error theory, ACA sample-size planning, ML data-requirement estimation and GP learning curves. The empirical benchmark is solid and publishable once the contribution is reframed. That means presenting the benchmark and the negative result as the main contribution, crediting prior art, and adding prior-art baselines: the Wei et al. exponent estimator, type-II ML on the full design, and a meta-learned or corrected power law. It also means testing a statistical noise-floor estimator before claiming that pilots cannot reveal the noise floor.
